Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Airline Pilot
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 79

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Proximity: Physical proximity, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Vignette:
Rangi Taumata is a 39-year-old New Zealand-born Māori man who works as a commercial airline pilot for a domestic carrier based in the Pacific Northwest. He is divorced, lives alone in a rented apartment near the airport, and presented for psychological assessment after his airline's employee assistance programme flagged a pattern of sick-day usage that had become difficult to conceal. His PCL-5 score of 79 places him in a range indicating severe posttraumatic stress, and the story he told across his first three sessions makes that severity comprehensible.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Rangi was driving a colleague home after an evening shift when he was pulled over on a freeway off-ramp. What began as a routine traffic stop escalated within seconds. Two officers approached the vehicle simultaneously, one on each side, and before Rangi had finished lowering his window the officer at his door had drawn his weapon and was shouting commands that contradicted those coming from the other side of the car. Rangi froze. His colleague, panicking, reached across him — a movement the officer at the driver's window interpreted as threatening. Rangi found himself pinned against the door, his face pressed into the frame, the cold barrel of a firearm against the back of his neck, screaming in his ears, his body entirely outside his control. He was certain, in those seconds, that he was about to die. The stop was eventually resolved without injury; a case of mistaken vehicle identity was cited. No formal complaint was pursued. Rangi drove home that night, showered, and told no one.

In the weeks that followed, the memory refused to behave like an ordinary memory. It did not recede with distance. When it returned — and it returned often — it arrived with the full physiological weight of the original moment: the same constriction in his chest, the same wave of nausea rising without warning, the same absolute certainty of imminent death. He described it to his therapist as less like remembering and more like being pulled back through a hole in time. What disturbed him almost as much as the intrusions themselves was the quality of the memory — sharper, more saturated, more real than anything else in his life. He had come to believe that the event had done something permanent to his mind, that a person whose memory worked this way was not a person who could be trusted with an aircraft full of passengers. At the same time, the memory felt so extreme, so far outside anything his life had contained before, that there were moments when he struggled to accept it had happened to him at all.

His threat monitoring had reorganised itself around the specific geometry of that night. He became acutely sensitive to proximity — anyone standing or sitting too close produced a tightening across his shoulders that he could not reason away. Strangers approaching him in ordinary settings, a gate agent walking briskly toward him, a passenger stopping to ask a question, registered as something requiring urgent assessment. Ordinary sounds — a door slamming, a trolley wheel catching on tile — produced a startle response he found humiliating in a professional context. When preflight checks ran long, or when air traffic control issued a hold instruction, he noticed a spike of dread that something terrible was unfolding just beyond his awareness. He had come to interpret unexplained delays as signals rather than inconveniences.

The most concrete occupational consequence had developed gradually. Rangi had begun avoiding the crew shuttle, the shared van that transported pilots and cabin staff between the terminal and the aircraft. Driving with other people in a confined vehicle had become intolerable. He had fabricated a series of reasons — early arrivals, equipment checks — to justify driving separately, but the logistics were becoming unsustainable, and a senior captain had begun asking questions. The nausea that accompanied any enclosed journey with others was now anticipated so reliably that it had begun to appear before he even boarded.

What finally brought Rangi into the room was a near-miss of a different kind: he had sat in the left-hand seat of a parked aircraft, alone on the ground, and found himself unable to begin the checklist. He sat there for eleven minutes. He has not told anyone what those eleven minutes contained. What he is most afraid of is that the answer, once spoken aloud, will end his career. What he is most hoping for is that it will not.
